title: Etana, Standard Babylonian Tablet III: the flight to heaven
source: British Museum tablet photographs + eBL manuscript transliterations (eBL corpus edition L I.9, Etana, SB III) + English of the eBL edition (B. R. Foster (eBL edition))
description: The Legend of Etana, Standard Babylonian Tablet III: 131 of 131 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (5 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.
introduction:
Etana rescues the eagle and, after a series of dreams, rides on its back towards the heaven of Anu. The text breaks off.

The Legend of Etana tells of an early king of Kish, chosen by the gods, who has no son. An eagle that betrayed its friend the serpent is thrown into a pit; Etana rescues it, and the eagle carries him up towards heaven to find the plant of birth. The story is known from Old Babylonian, Middle Assyrian and Standard Babylonian versions; the end is lost. This page follows the line numbering of the electronic Babylonian Library edition.

How this page is built. Each section is a run of consecutive lines as written on one photographed clay tablet. For every line the eBL edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/9/SB/III) lists the manuscripts that carry it, with each tablet's own column and line numbers; the tablet chosen for each run is the photographed copy of the work with the most signs preserved there. Commentaries and texts that only quote a line are never chosen. School and excerpt tablets are used only for lines that no photographed library copy preserves as well, and only where they carry the line as text; their sections say so. The original text is eBL's transliteration of that tablet's signs (not a modern composite text): square brackets mark broken signs, x an illegible sign, # a damaged sign, ? an uncertain reading, and words in {braces} are determinatives; the notes give a key to every sign used on this page, and eBL's layout codes are written out in words (for example '(line break)' or '(blank space)'). Superscript numbers are the line numbers of the eBL edition, used in both the Akkadian and the English. The English is B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), one line of English per line of the text; italics mark uncertain renderings, as in the source. Where the tablet is broken, the English still translates the whole line of eBL's composite text; each section's note names the lines that are broken on its tablet.

Finding a line on the photograph. Each section names the tablet, the face and column, and the tablet's own line numbers (a prime, as in 5', counts from the first preserved line of a broken column). On a tablet with six columns the obverse carries columns i-iii from left to right; the reverse, turned over from bottom to top, carries columns iv-vi from right to left. The photographs often show the obverse above the reverse with the edges around them; a fragment preserves only part of this layout.

This page shows 131 of the 131 lines of the eBL edition (100%), from 5 tablets in the British Museum: K.2606 (Nineveh), K.3651 (Nineveh), K.19530 (Nineveh), 1882,0323.6 (Nineveh), K.8563 (Nineveh).
translator_notes: Akkadian: eBL transliteration of the signs on the photographed tablet (manuscript-level ATF), not a composite text.
English: B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition; it renders eBL's composite text, including restorations from other tablets.
Line numbers: eBL edition. Each section also gives the tablet's own column and line numbers.

Signs in the Akkadian: [ ] broken away; x illegible sign; # damaged sign; ? uncertain reading; ! sign corrected by the editor; * collated sign; ... broken signs of unknown number; ( ) signs perhaps broken away; { } determinative; / alternative readings; : divider sign written on the tablet; (blank space) a space left by the scribe.

translation.text: <sup>1</sup>The eagle made ready to speak, say[ing] to Shamash his lord,
translation.scan_note: British Museum K.2606: column iv, the tablet's own line 4'. eBL's corpus edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/9/SB/III) attributes SB III 1 to this manuscript at these column and line numbers. Photograph checked: obverse, reverse and edges, ink number K.2606 on the edge; a column of about 29 lines on the obverse and a few lines on the reverse, consistent with eBL's attribution. K.2606, a copy of SB I, carries this line as its catch-line: the opening of the next tablet of the series, copied at the end of the previous one (eBL lists catch-lines among its quotations; unlike commentaries and quotations in other texts, a catch-line is the line itself on a copy of the work). On this tablet line 1 is partly broken (square brackets and x in the Akkadian). The English of this line translates eBL's composite text, so it includes words that are not preserved on this tablet but are restored from other manuscripts or by the editors. Square brackets in the English mark eBL's restorations in its composite text; words that survive on other tablets carry no brackets even where this tablet is broken.

2“My [lord], ... [...],
3“[... him] the speech of birds,
4“Although I am [an eagle and he is a human being],
5“[What]ever he will sa[y, let me understand],
6“[Wha]tever I will say, [let him understand].”
7According to the command of Shamash the warr[ior ...],
8[Etana could understand] the speech of birds.
9The eagle made read[y to] speak, saying [to E]tana,
10“Why is it that you have come here [this w]ay?”
11Etana made read[y to] speak, saying [to the ea]gle,
12“Friend, give me the [pl]ant of birth!
13“Reveal to me the [pl]ant of birth!
14“[Relieve me] of my disgrace, give me an [he]ir!
15“[...] left behind [... the plan]t of birth!
16“It comes out [where] the birds fly forth,
17“[That is why I have come] this way.”
18“I alone can [...] the mountains,
19“I will bring you [the plant of b]irth.”
20He went and [... the mountains alone],
21The eagle hunted [...],
22[The plant of birth] was not there.
23“Come, my friend, [...],
24“[The plant of birth is] with the lady, [...] Ishtar.
25“[We must go] to Ishtar, the lady [...].
26“[Put your arms] against my sides,
27“[Put your hands] against my wing feathers.”
28He put [his arms] against his sides,
29[He put his hands] against his wing feathers.
30[When he had borne him aloft] one league,
31“Look, my friend, how the land [is now]!”

translation.text:
b+15The eagle [said] to him, to Etana,
b+16“My friend, [your] dre[ams] are obvious!
b+17“Come, let me take you up to heaven [of Anu].
b+18“Put [your chest] against my chest,
b+19“Put [your hands] against my wing feathers,
b+20“Put [your arms] against my sides.”
b+21He put [his chest] against his chest,
b+22He put [his] hands against his wing feathers,
b+23He put [his] hands against his sides,
b+24Great indeed was the burden upon him.
b+25When he bore [him] aloft one league,
b+26The eagle said to him, to Etana,
b+27“Look, my friend, how the land is now!
b+28“Examine the sea, look for its boundaries.”
b+29“The land stretches to the mountains,
b+30“The sea has become a stream.”
b+31When he had borne him aloft a second league,
b+32The eagle said to him, to Etana,
b+33“Look, my friend, how the land is now!”
b+34“The land is watery.”
b+35When he had borne him aloft a third league,
b+36The eagle said to him, to Etana,
b+37“Look, my friend, how the land i[s now]!”
b+38“The sea has become a gard[ener]’s ditch.”
b+39After they had ascended to the heaven of A[nu],
b+40[They] passed through the gates of Anu, Enlil, and Ea.
b+41The eagle and E[tana] did obei[sance to]gether.

On this tablet lines b+15-b+23, b+25-b+28, b+31-b+32, b+34, b+36-b+41 are partly broken (square brackets and x in the Akkadian). The English of these lines translates eBL's composite text, so it includes words that are not preserved on this tablet but are restored from other manuscripts or by the editors. Square brackets in the English mark eBL's restorations in its composite text; words that survive on other tablets carry no brackets even where this tablet is broken. Lines b+24, b+29-b+30, b+33, b+35 are complete on this tablet.

translation.scan_note: British Museum K.3651: reverse, the tablet's own lines 9' to 12' and 21' to 27'. eBL's corpus edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/9/SB/III) attributes SB III b+42-c+7 to this manuscript at these column and line numbers. Photograph checked: obverse, reverse and edges of the join K.3651 + K.8578 (ink numbers on the edges); a long column on the obverse and text on the reverse, consistent with eBL's obverse (39 lines) and reverse (19 lines). eBL numbers these lines on the tablet 9' to 12' and 21' to 27': its line numbers jump although the poem lines are consecutive. On this tablet of lines c+1-c+3 only illegible traces (x) survive, of lines b+43-b+45, c+4-c+5, c+7 only one to three signs survive and lines b+42, c+6 are partly broken (square brackets and x in the Akkadian). The English of these lines translates eBL's composite text, so it includes words that are not preserved on this tablet but are restored from other manuscripts or by the editors. Square brackets in the English mark eBL's restorations in its composite text; words that survive on other tablets carry no brackets even where this tablet is broken.
